results.blind_working: A large plastic region between elastic limit and fracture means ductile, so P is ductile. Fracture just after the elastic limit means brittle, so Q is brittle.

Stress is force/area, so its unit is N/m², the same as pressure, and A is true. Strain is a ratio of lengths and dimensionless, so R is true. R explains strain, not why stress has the unit of pressure, so it is not the explanation of A.
Hooke's law holds only up to the proportional limit, so I is false. Rubber is an elastomer with a large elastic region and no well-defined plastic region, so II is false.
Fluids cannot sustain shear stress or a definite length, so they have no rigidity or Young's modulus. They resist volume change, so they have bulk modulus only.
Extension under own weight is ΔL = ρgL²/(2Y), which does not depend on radius. Y has length 2L, so ΔL_Y/ΔL_X = (2L)²/L² = 4.

Young's modulus relates to change in length (IV). Bulk modulus relates to change in volume (III). Modulus of rigidity relates to change in shape (I). Compressibility is the reciprocal of bulk modulus (II).

A is true in the standard textbook sense: G = Y/(2(1+σ)), giving G ≈ Y/3 for typical σ. B is true: Poisson's ratio is dimensionless with theoretical range -1 to 0.5. C is false: Y is a material property, independent of length. D is true: energy density = stress²/(2Y). E is false: a thicker wire has larger area, so it extends less. Correct set is A, B and D.
Gauge pressure P = ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 5 = 5×10^4 Pa.
F2 = F1(A2/A1) = 200 × 50 = 10^4 N. Volume is conserved, so d2 = d1(A1/A2) = 25/50 = 0.5 cm.
Pressure at the base is P = ρgh. It depends only on depth, not on vessel shape, so it is the same in all three (hydrostatic paradox).
Pascal's law gives equal pressure on both pistons, so F2 = F1A2/A1. This is exactly why a small force supports a large load, so R correctly explains A.
An open-tube manometer measures P − Patm, which is gauge pressure, so I is true. 1 atm = 1.013 bar > 1 bar, and NCERT defines 1 torr = 1 mm Hg, so II is true.
An orbiting spacecraft is in free fall, so the effective g is zero. With no hydrostatic pressure gradient, there is no buoyant force.
g_eff = g + a = 12 m/s^2. P = rho*g_eff*h = 1000 x 12 x 0.5 = 6000 Pa.
tan(theta) = a/g = 5/10 = 1/2, so theta = tan^-1(1/2).
At rest: rho*g*h. Upward acceleration: rho(g+a)h. Downward acceleration: rho(g-a)h. Free fall: zero. This gives A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I.

A is true (dP/dh = rho*g). B is false: air is compressible and pressure falls roughly exponentially. C is false: the submerged fraction is independent of g_eff. D is true (buoyancy arises from the gravity-induced pressure difference). E is true (no depth-dependent pressure in free fall).
From F = ηA(dv/dx), η = F/(A·dv/dx). This gives [MLT^-2]/([L^2][T^-1]) = [ML^-1T^-1].
Volume is conserved, so R^3 = 8r^3 and R = 2r. Terminal velocity scales as r^2, so v = 4 × 5 = 20 cm/s.
Terminal velocity is proportional to r^2, so the larger ball falls faster. A is false and R is true.

At terminal velocity, drag plus buoyancy equals weight, so drag equals weight only if buoyancy is neglected. I is therefore incorrect. v = (2r^2ρg/9η)(σ/ρ - 1) is linear in σ/ρ and zero at σ/ρ = 1, so II is correct.
In streamline (steady) flow, the velocity at a given point stays constant in time. Streamlines never cross, and the flow has no eddies.
Re = ρvD/η = 1000 × 0.2 × 0.02 / 1e-3 = 4000. Since Re > 3000, the flow is turbulent.

Reynolds number is the ratio of inertial to viscous force (A-III). Critical velocity is the speed beyond which flow turns turbulent (B-IV). Continuity expresses mass conservation (C-II). Crowded streamlines mark higher speed (D-I).
Critical velocity vc = Re·η/(ρD). A is true (vc rises with η). B is false (vc falls with D). C is true (Re is dimensionless). D is true (Av is constant). E is false (vc falls with ρ).
By Torricelli's law, v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2 × 10 × 5) = sqrt(100) = 10 m/s.
Hole depth h = 0.5 m, so its height above ground is 2.5 − 0.5 = 2.0 m. Range R = 2·sqrt(h(H−h)) = 2·sqrt(0.5 × 2.0) = 2·sqrt(1) = 2.0 m.
Continuity: v2 = 1 × 10/5 = 2 m/s. Bernoulli: ΔP = ½ρ(v2² − v1²) = 0.5 × 1000 × (4 − 1) = 1500 Pa.
By continuity, speed is higher where the section is narrower, so R is true. Bernoulli then gives lower pressure at the narrow section, so A is false.

I: each term of Bernoulli's equation is energy per unit volume, with the dimensions of pressure, so I is true. II: range = 2·sqrt(d(H−d)). At d = H/4, range = 2·sqrt(3H²/16) = 0.866H. At d = H/2, range = H, which is the maximum. So II is false.
Surface tension is force per length (N/m). This equals energy per area: J/m^2 = N·m/m^2 = N/m.
A soap film has two surfaces, so W = 2TΔA = 2 × 0.03 × (30 × 10^-4 m^2) = 1.8 × 10^-4 J.
The film pulls on the wire along both surfaces, so F = 2TL = 2 × 0.04 × 0.05 = 4.0 × 10^-3 N.

Pure water on clean glass has contact angle about 0° (IV). Mercury on glass is about 140° (II). Detergent lowers both surface tension and contact angle (III). NaCl, being highly soluble, raises surface tension (I).
A is false: surface tension does not depend on area. B, C and D are true. E is false: when cohesion exceeds adhesion, the contact angle is obtuse.
A soap bubble has two surfaces, so ΔP = 4S/R = 4(0.03)/0.02 = 6 Pa.
An air bubble in water has one surface. P = P0 + ρgh + 2S/r = 1e5 + 1000 + 1400 = 1.024e5 Pa.
Interface radius r = r1·r2/(r2 − r1) = 24/2 = 12 cm.
Excess pressure 4S/R is larger in the smaller bubble, so air flows from small to large and A is true. R is false because ΔP is inversely proportional to R.

In vacuum, isothermal: ΣPV is conserved, so Σr² is conserved, giving r = √(9+16) = 5 cm, not 7 cm. Statement I is false. A cylindrical surface gives ΔP = S/R, half of 2S/R for a drop, so Statement II is true.
By Jurin's law h ∝ 1/r. Halving the radius doubles the rise: 6 × 2 = 12 cm.

A: h ∝ 1/r, so the rise doubles (I). B: effective g = 0, so liquid rises to the full tube length (II). C: mercury in glass has an obtuse contact angle, so it is depressed with a convex meniscus (III). D: in a short tube hR stays constant, so the meniscus radius grows and there is no overflow (IV).

A is true: S is larger at lower temperature, so the rise is greater. B is false: only half the work, πrSh, is stored as potential energy; the rest is lost as heat. C is true: merging reduces surface area, releasing energy. D is true: an acute contact angle gives a concave meniscus. E is false: each droplet has radius R/27^(1/3) = R/3. Correct set is A, C, D.
Stress = Y x alpha x dT = 2e11 x 1.2e-5 x 50 = 1.2e8 N/m^2.
Time lost per day = (1/2) x alpha x dT x 86400 = 0.5 x 2e-5 x 20 x 86400 = 17.28 s.
A is true and R is true. A is explained by water's anomalous expansion (maximum density at 4 deg C) and ice's low conductivity, not by its high specific heat.
I is false: the metal with larger alpha ends up on the convex side, so the strip bends towards the metal with smaller alpha. II is true: volume coefficient is 3 alpha, so rho' ≈ rho(1 - 3 alpha dT).
Heat lost by block = heat gained by water: 200(0.25)(100 − T) = 200(1)(T − 20). This gives 5000 − 50T = 200T − 4000, so 250T = 9000 and T = 36°C.
Water cooling from 30°C to 0°C releases 200 × 30 = 6000 cal. Melting all the ice needs 100 × 80 = 8000 cal. Since 6000 < 8000, only part of the ice melts and the mixture stays at 0°C.
Isothermal: heat flows with no temperature change, so C is infinite (II). Adiabatic: no heat flows, so C is zero (III). Cp − Cv = R (I). Water: 1 cal/g°C (IV). So A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV.

A is true: water equivalent = mc/c_w. B is true: calorimetry rests on energy conservation. C is true: ice is about 0.5 cal/g°C. D is false: for an ideal gas Cp > Cv. E is false: heat for unit mass is specific heat, not heat capacity. So A, B and C only.
Cooling 200 g of water from 30°C to 0°C releases 200×1×30 = 6000 cal. Melting all the ice would need 100×80 = 8000 cal. Since 6000 < 8000, only 6000/80 = 75 g melts, leaving 25 g of ice at 0°C.
With constant power P, P = m c (dT/dt). So c_s·4 = c_l·2, giving c_s/c_l = 1/2. Latent heat is proportional to plateau time, so L_v/L_f = 12/3 = 4.
A is true: higher pressure raises the boiling point above 100°C. R is true: pressure lowers the melting point of ice (regelation). R concerns melting, not boiling, so it does not explain A.

I is correct: at constant temperature the heat absorbed goes into potential energy, not kinetic energy. II is incorrect: water's fusion curve has a negative slope, so pressure lowers the melting point.
Equal heat current through both slabs: K(100 − T) = 2K(T − 10). So 100 − T = 2T − 20, giving T = 40 °C.
First stage: 20/5 = k(70 − 20), so 4 = 50k and k = 0.08 per min. Second stage: 30/t = 0.08(45 − 20) = 2, so t = 15 min.
K has units W m^-1 K^-1 (IV). b has units m K (I). σ has units W m^-2 K^-4 (II). L/(KA) has units K W^-1 (III).

A is true: the harmonic-mean result for equal lengths. B is true: P ∝ T^4 gives 16×, and λmax ∝ 1/T halves. C is false: Newton's law is linear in excess temperature. D is false: good absorbers are good emitters. E is true: sea breeze is natural convection. So A, B and E.
